newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Pace tightens for reform in Russian car wars.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Pace tightens for reform in Russian car wars.

text.p: Russia's huge auto industry, wary of reform and frightened of competition, must fight for survival as Western manufacturers seek to enter the domestic market, analysts said this week.
The experts, attending an auto industry conference, said Russia's car and truck makers still gave priority to quantity over quality in Soviet-style five-year plans.

Russian firms, which gained a reputation for shoddy models in Soviet days, still make up the largest auto industry in formerly communist central and eastern Europe, employing over half a million people.
But Russia is the only carmaking country in the region where no foreign carmakers own shares in domestic manufacturers.
"Russian managers can still be arrogant, and many are wary of Western automakers and banks," said Richard Hanna, a partner at Price Waterhouse in Moscow.
"They tend to look at the future with rose-tinted glasses because the severity of their crises still hasn't hit them. They haven't had a reality check."

Analysts said Russian auto firms, exposed to tough competition in their home market, faced certain demise without outside capital, expertise and technology. Production has fallen 24 percent for cars and 77 percent for trucks since 1990.
"Such a drop in production is lethal," said Dagmar Bottenbruch, research director for MC Securities Ltd in London.

"The worst companies will probably continue to exist for some time for political reasons...but we don't believe Western automakers should invest large sums of money in this risky environment. Only a fully restructured company would be interesting, and none exist in the Russian auto industry."
Industry sources said Russian automakers were averse to Western investor requirements, such as cutting capacity and employment.

But the day of reckoning is nearing. Several local automakers have halted output for periods in recent years due to problems with equipment, suppliers or workers. Some face the threat of bankruptcy proceedings due to big tax debts.
"It will be really difficult for Russian automakers to become competitive until they have some financial liquidity," Bottenbruch said.

Old habits die hard, however. AO Gorkovsky Avtomobilny Zavod, Russia's second-largest automaker, outlined plans at the conference for a collection of new cars and trucks without discussing their financial feasibility.
"Automakers across the world are cutting costs by cutting down the number of models and parts they use," Hanna said. "But Russian automakers are heading in the opposite direction."
Russian automakers are reluctant to downsize because it would involve politically sensitive actions like sacking workers, but analysts said overemployment was one of their biggest problems.
Russian firms are highly inefficient in terms of cars made per employee.

But Russia, which has 80 cars per 1,000 residents compared to 560 in the United States, offers enormous opportunities. "The Russian market and its potential is simply too big to ignore," Bottenbruch said.
Foreign automakers, including Daewoo Group and Kia Motors Corp of Korea, GM, and Skoda automobilova AS of the Czech Republic, have already opted to assemble cars in Russia.

But some Russian firms are making changes. AvtoVAZ abandoned grand schemes to raise nearly $6 billion for new models and has started work with Finnish bodywork specialist Valmet Automotive Inc, to upgrade the outdated Samara car for western Europe.
"I've seen a lot of changes at AvtoVAZ," said Hanna of Price Waterhouse, which advises them. "They are trying to implement modern production methods, and look like they have a chance."
